body_excerpt: ## Goal Add a machine-readable JSON output mode to `sorseal analyze` (mirroring the existing `verify --json` pattern) so findings can be consumed by scripts, CI gates, dashboards, and other tooling. `--json` should emit a single JSON document to stdout describing the analysis: project, artifact, the rule set, every finding (rule id, severity, file, line, message, remediation), the per-severity counts, and the analysis digest. ## Scope - Add `-f json` / `--format json` support to the `analyze` subcommand in `src/main.rs`. - Emit a deterministic document: order findings by rule → file → line (the same order used to compute the digest in `src/analyze.rs`) so output is stable. - Fields should round-trip cleanly; reuse `Severity` and `RuleId` display names. - Add a unit test in `src/analyze.rs` asserting the JSON structure and that the digest matches the one produced by the console summary. ## Why `analyze` produces human output today. Teams want to gate CI on findings (see the `--fail-on` issue) and slice findings by severity/file in scripts. JSON is the lowest-common-denominator format for that. ## Success criteria - `sorseal analyze --format json` prints a valid JSON document (all severities present). - Running on the bundled `examples/vulnerable-contract` yields the same findings/digest as the console output. - `cargo test --locked`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` all pass.
title: good-first-issue: sorseal analyze --format json

body_excerpt: ## Goal Let teams run `sorseal analyze` in CI as a real gate by failing on findings at or above a chosen severity, e.g. `--fail-on Critical` or `--fail-on High`. Today the command always reports findings but does not exit non-zero based on severity, so a repo can't turn "no Criticals" into a CI failure. ## Scope - Add `--fail-on <Critical|High|Medium|Low>` to the `analyze` subcommand in `src/main.rs`. - If any finding has severity >= the threshold, exit with a non-zero status (use the existing exit-code convention for "checks failed"). Otherwise exit 0. - When `--fail-on` is not supplied, keep the current behavior (report only). - Print a clear summary line when the gate trips, e.g. `FAIL: 3 findings at or above High severity`. - Wire the threshold comparison into an `Analysis` helper (e.g. reuse `count_by_severity` / severity ordering in `src/analyze.rs`) and unit-test it. ## Why Static analysis is only useful in an audit workflow if it can block bad builds. This makes `sorseal analyze` immediately usable as a pre-merge gate in the GitHub Action (`action.yml`) and standalone CI, and pairs naturally with the `--json` output. ## Success criteria - `sorseal analyze --fail-on High` on `examples/vulnerable-contract` exits non-zero. - `sorseal analyze --fail-on Critical` still exits non-zero there; `--fail-on Low` does too. - `sorseal analyze` with no `--fail-on` exits 0 even when findings exist. - Tests, fmt, and clippy stay green.
title: good-first-issue: sorseal analyze --fail-on <severity>

body_excerpt: ## Goal Let teams suppress findings they have reviewed as acceptable, instead of blocking on them forever. Add a per-rule allowlist / inline suppression so a specific rule at a specific line can be silenced with a clear reason. Two clean surfaces (pick one or both; an issue should first implement inline `// sorseal:ignore <RULE>` comments): - Inline: `// sorseal:ignore SORSEAL-104 reviewed: panic unreachable` on the line above a finding suppresses that one. - Config: an optional `[analysis.ignore]` table in `sorseal.toml` listing `"rule": ["file:line"]` or `"rule"` (whole file) entries. ## Scope - Parse inline `// sorseal:ignore <RULE>` comments during the per-line scan in `src/analyze.rs` and drop matching findings. - Respect a `--no-ignore` flag that temporarily ignores suppressions (useful to see everything). - Since suppressions affect the finding set, the analysis digest (`Analysis::digest` in `src/analyze.rs`) must reflect suppressed findings removed, so a suppressed run seals a different digest than an unsuppressed one. - Add tests: a suppressed finding disappears, an unrelated-inline comment does not suppress, and removing the suppression changes the digest. ## Why Real audit workflows involve noise. False positives (or accepted risks with a written reason) currently force teams to either block forever or route around the tool. Inline, reason-carrying suppressions are the standard pattern (c.f. `clippy::allow`, Rustc `#[allow]`) and keep the audit trail honest by making the decision explicit and reviewable. ## Success criteria - A line tagged `// sorseal:ignore SORSEAL-104` produces no SORSEAL-104 finding. - `--no-ignore` restores it. - Suppressed findings are excluded from counts and from the sealed digest. - Tests, fmt, and clippy stay green.
title: good-first-issue: inline/config suppressions for analyze findings

body_excerpt: ## Goal Add a `--explain <RULE>` flag to `sorseal analyze` that prints human-readable guidance for a detection rule without running an analysis — what it covers, why it matters for Soroban contracts, and how to fix it. Example: ```text $ sorseal analyze --explain SORSEAL-101 SORSEAL-101 missing-authorization (Critical) Detects a function that mutates contract state or moves value without calling `require_auth` first ... Example fix: ...use `env.current_contract_address` / `require_auth`... ``` ## Scope - Add `--explain` handling in `src/main.rs` (print and exit; no scan). - Define a durable description + remediation text per rule. The remediation is already a field on `Finding`; promote a static rule-metadata table in `src/analyze.rs` (id → name, severity, long description, example, how-to-fix) and have both `--explain` and the SARIF rule definitions (`src/sarif.rs`) read from it, so descriptions stay in one place. - List all rules when `--explain` is given without a value, or with `--explain all`. - Unit-test that every known `RuleId` has an entry in the table. ## Why Repos that adopt an analyzer gate need to teach contributors *why* a finding is flagged and *how* to fix it. A self-contained `--explain` turns the CLI into its own documentation and keeps the rule set approachable for newcomers — good for adoption and for `good-first-issue` contributors. ## Success criteria - `sorseal analyze --explain SORSEAL-101` prints a non-empty, useful description + fix for every defined rule. - `--explain` with no rule prints the full rule list. - No source scan runs when `--explain` is used. - Tests, fmt, and clippy stay green.
title: good-first-issue: sorseal analyze --explain <RULE>

body_excerpt: ## Goal Add a bundled **golden-file test harness** for `sorseal analyze` so rule changes can't silently alter which findings are reported or break the sealed digest. A golden file records the full expected finding set (rule, severity, file, line) for the bundled `examples/vulnerable-contract`. Running `sorseal analyze` must reproduce exactly that set and the same digest, or the test fails. ## Scope - Add an integration test (in `tests/`) that runs `sorseal analyze` against `examples/vulnerable-contract` and compares the finding set + analysis digest to a checked-in golden JSON (e.g. `tests/fixtures/analyze/vulnerable-contract.json`). - Provide a `--update-golden` style helper (or an env flag) that regenerates the golden file when a rule change *intentionally* alters output, so updating is a deliberate, reviewed step rather than an automatic fix. - Test failure output should show the diff between expected and actual findings. - Wire the test into `cargo test` so it runs in CI. ## Why `analyze` claims a *stable, tamper-evident* digest, and the finding set must stay deterministic across rule iterations (`SORSEAL-105` activation, suppressions, and new rules all risk drifting). Golden tests lock the contract, and they are a perfect, low-risk first contribution that protects the audit guarantee. ## Success criteria - The golden test passes on an unmodified tree. - Editing `examples/vulnerable-contract` (e.g. adding a finding) makes the test fail with a clear diff; regenerating with the helper and re-running passes. - `cargo test --locked`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass.
title: good-first-issue: golden-file digest tests for analyze

body_excerpt: ## Goal Expand detection coverage for the newest security-relevant rule: catch **unchecked / balance-insensitive transfers** (SORSEAL-105, currently dormant) so `analyze` flags the classic Soroban drain where a function transfers a token balance without first reading/checking the contract's actual balance or a guaranteed allowance. ```rust // currently NOT flagged: fn sweep(env: Env, to: Address) { let amount = SOME_CONSTANT; // no balance read token::Client::new(&env, &to).transfer(&env.current_contract_address(), &to, &amount); } ``` ## Scope - Finalize `SORSEAL-105` in `src/analyze.rs`: detect a token `.transfer(...)` (or `.transfer_from(...)`) call that is not preceded in its function by a `ledger().balance(...)` / allowance read of the same contract, indicating the amount is hard-coded or derived without checking available balance. - Reuse the existing per-function analysis (see SORSEAL-102's state-mutation tracking) so the check is function-scoped, not just line-scoped. - Assign severity (propose **High**); add a remediation string. - Add a vulnerable snippet + a benign snippet (one that does read balance first) to the test fixtures in `src/analyze.rs` and assert only the vulnerable one fires. - Uncomment/register the rule in the rule table (`src/analyze.rs` `RuleId` / severity mapping) and update the console + SARIF + Markdown renderers if they enumerate rules. ## Why Missing balance/allowance checks are a leading cause of Soroban value loss. Activating SORSEAL-105 gives `analyze` real, new findings on a class the current rule set mostly misses, strengthening the vulnerability-scan story. ## Success criteria - The vulnerable snippet yields a SORSEAL-105 finding; the balance-checked snippet does not. - Rule appears in `--explain` output and SARIF rules. - `cargo test --locked`, `cargo fmt --check`, `cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings` pass.
title: good-first-issue: activate SORSEAL-105 unchecked-transfer detection

body_excerpt: ### Target File or Module crates/pec-core/src/math/q64.rs ### Background and Context The PEC protocol mandates deterministic fixed-point mathematics (`PEC-MATH-01`) to prevent floating-point consensus forks across heterogeneous nodes (x86_64, ARM Cortex-M, and RISC-V), as established in `docs/adr/0001-deterministic-q64-fixed-point-math.md`. The foundational numerical primitive is the signed Q64.64 fixed-point integer, where values are represented as a signed 128-bit integer with 64 fractional bits: $$X = x \cdot 2^{-64}, \quad x \in [-2^{127}, 2^{127}-1]$$ Consensus safety requires that addition and subtraction do not wrap modulo $2^{128}$; instead, they must saturate at numeric boundaries. ### Step-by-Step Implementation Guide 1. Define the core `Q64` tuple struct wrapping `i128`: ```rust #[derive(Copy, Clone, Debug, Default, PartialEq, Eq, PartialOrd, Ord, Hash)] pub struct Q64(pub i128); ``` 2. Implement numeric boundary constants on `Q64`: * `Q64::MAX = Q64(i128::MAX)` (representing approximately $9.223372036854775807 \times 10^{18}$) * `Q64::MIN = Q64(i128::MIN)` (representing approximately $-9.223372036854775808 \times 10^{18}$) * `Q64::ZERO = Q64(0)` * `Q64::ONE = Q64(1i128 << 64)` 3. We have a public Base payout address and can produce research/browser/code deliverables, but we will not expose private keys or manufacture self-dealing GMV. The current ready-to-earn GitHub discovery results we found are dominated by GMV competitions that require entrant-funded child bounties. We are specifically looking for a genuinely externally funded solver opportunity with zero required external spend and a bounded/replayable acceptance test. Could a maintainer point us to the current canonical opportunity (if one exists) that best satisfies: - claimable/ready-to-earn now; - Base USDC escrow already funded by an independent poster; - AI-agent participation allowed; - no external spend required by the solver; - research, browser, documentation, or small-code scope; - deterministic or otherwise replayable acceptance evidence; - no requirement that the solver fund another bounty or create circular activity. If no such inventory is currently live, a direct “none live right now” answer is useful; we do not want to manufacture activity merely to qualify for a prize. Project: https://github.com/jain-Igtm/CashGPT This is an onboarding/inventory question, not a claim or representation that payment has been earned.

Therefore: ```text parent gross profit = parent solver reward - child funding cost <= 0 ``` Lowering the bond while preserving that verifier would create a cheaper but still economically irrational bounty. body_excerpt: Add a small MQTT output adapter that can publish serialized `MachineEvent` payloads without requiring access to a CNC. Suggested scope: - create a focused publisher interface/module; - keep MQTT as an optional dependency; - publish the existing `MachineEvent.to_dict()` payload without changing the event schema; - make broker URL/topic configurable; - do not log credentials; - add unit tests using a fake/mocked client; - add a short usage example in docs. Out of scope: commanding a machine, PLC writes, production credentials, or real factory infrastructure. Acceptance criteria: - unit tests pass in CI; - no network access is required for tests; - failure to publish is surfaced clearly; - docs include one local-broker example.
title: Good first issue: add MQTT event output adapter

body_excerpt: Add a small HTTP webhook adapter for publishing serialized `MachineEvent` payloads. Suggested scope: - keep HTTP client dependency optional; - accept a target URL and timeout; - POST `MachineEvent.to_dict()` as JSON; - support simple static headers without exposing secrets in logs; - add tests with a fake/mocked client; - document retry/error behavior without building a large queueing system. Acceptance criteria: - no real network is required in CI; - clear errors on non-2xx responses/timeouts; - credentials/tokens are not printed; - one minimal usage example is documented. Out of scope: machine control, authentication frameworks, persistent delivery queues.
title: Good first issue: add webhook event output adapter

body_excerpt: Write a practical deployment guide for running the lightweight FactoryLens components on a Raspberry Pi-class edge device. Suggested scope: - supported/expected Python setup; - virtual environment and optional dependency installation; - RTSP network considerations; - FFmpeg installation notes; - storage layout and log locations; - what should *not* be expected on low-power hardware (for example heavy multi-camera inference); - example systemd service file or equivalent process-management guidance. Acceptance criteria: - new documentation page under `docs/`; - commands are copyable and avoid hard-coded credentials; - clearly distinguish tested guidance from assumptions if no Pi hardware is available; - link the guide from README or another docs index. No CNC hardware is required for this contribution.
title: Good first issue: add Raspberry Pi deployment guide

body_excerpt: Improve `JobContextNormalizer` coverage for common Indonesian-spoken material names without weakening ambiguity safeguards. Suggested scope: - add a small set of well-defined aliases for existing or newly documented canonical materials; - include spoken-letter/number variants where useful; - add positive and ambiguity tests; - do not silently guess when two canonical materials match; - document every new canonical material/alias pair. Useful examples to consider: additional carbon-steel grades, stainless grades, aluminium naming variants, and common operator pronunciations. Acceptance criteria: - all aliases are deterministic; - ambiguous phrases remain `ready=False`; - tests cover each added alias; - no external speech service is required. Please keep the first PR intentionally small (roughly 5–10 canonical/alias additions).

body_excerpt: Welcome! 🥳 This is the landing issue for anyone who wants to make a first contribution to Boost.Graph. Every task below is small, self-contained, and reviewable in one sitting. They are real cleanups we want done, not busywork. Tasks are grouped into three tiers by the C++ background they actually require, so you can pick one that matches where you are. - Tier 1 needs nothing beyond being able to read code - Tier 3 assumes you know what the old workaround was working around. ## How to claim a task 1. Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/boostorg/graph/blob/develop/CONTRIBUTING.md) first: it has the superproject setup, the build and test commands, the naming conventions, and the full `BOOST_*` macro policy table that several tasks below refer to. 2. Comment on this issue saying which box you are taking, e.g. *"Taking 2.1 on `strong_components.hpp`"*. We will tick it here so nobody duplicates work. 3. Ask questions in the comments. There is no such thing as a question too basic on this issue. ## Ground rules - **One file per PR.** Every checkbox below is exactly one file and exactly one PR. This is deliberate: small PRs get reviewed much faster, they are easy to revert if we got something wrong, and they let many people contribute in parallel without stepping on each other. Please do not batch several files together to "save time" as it costs review time. The one exception is a header and its matching test when the change genuinely spans both. - **One task per PR.** Several files appear under more than one task. If your file needs work from two tasks, that is two PRs. Do not mix a macro cleanup with a rename or a formatting pass. - **No behavior change.** Everything below should be a no-op at runtime. If you find a bug along the way, that is great: open a separate PR, with a regression test. - **The test suite must stay green.** `./b2` from `libs/graph/test` runs everything (~10 min). For a single test: `./b2 cycle_canceling_test`. If you struggle with local bui…

body_excerpt: # Implement Basic Application Health Check ## Description Create a simple health-check component that allows the Enterprise AI system to determine whether its core services are operational. This will provide a foundation for future monitoring, container orchestration, and production deployment. ### Tasks * [ ] Create a reusable `HealthCheck` interface/class. * [ ] Define basic health states such as: * `HEALTHY` * `DEGRADED` * `UNHEALTHY` * [ ] Implement a basic application health check. * [ ] Return a structured health status. * [ ] Add unit tests. * [ ] Document how the health check can be extended. ### Example ```cpp auto status = health_check.run(); if (status.is_healthy()) { std::cout << "System is healthy\n"; } ``` ### Expected Structure ```text HealthCheck │ ├── Application Health ├── AI Engine Health └── Infrastructure Health ``` The initial implementation does **not** need to implement database, network, or external-service checks. Those can be introduced in future issues. ### Acceptance Criteria * [ ] Health-check component compiles successfully. * [ ] Basic health states are implemented. * [ ] Unit tests cover the health states. * [ ] The component is independent and reusable. * [ ] Documentation includes a usage example. ### Difficulty **Beginner-friendly** ### Labels `good first issue` `help wanted` `cpp` `health-check` `enhancement`

body_excerpt: ## Summary fund_bounty_pool(), fund_emergency_pool() and create_escrow() never receive or transfer any actual tokens. They only increment i128 counters stored in contract storage. There is no transfer of XLM or any SAC token, and no check that the caller actually holds/deposited funds. ## Severity Critical ## Location contracts/scanner/src/lib.rs - fund_bounty_pool(), fund_emergency_pool(), create_escrow() ## Impact - The bounty and emergency pools are pure accounting fiction. Any authenticated caller can call fund_bounty_pool() (it only requires funder.require_auth(); no role check, no balance check) and inflate BOUNTY_POOL arbitrarily. - verify_vulnerability() and emergency rewards then "pay out" from these pools without any real assets backing them - the contract can promise rewards it can never deliver (insolvency) or mint value out of thin air. ## Root Cause No token::Client transfer/import, no contract balance checks, and no relationship between the stored counters and any real asset balance. ## Recommended Fix - Integrate the Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) token interface and perform real transfers: transfer the funded amount into the contract on deposit, and out to the beneficiary on payout. - Require TreasuryManager role on fund_bounty_pool (parity with fund_emergency_pool) and assert the contract actually received the deposited amount. ## Bounty Note Broken token custody/accounting on a bounty platform is a direct economic exploit with high reward.

body_excerpt: ## Why UI Iceberg v0.2 can plan journeys and reconcile Playwright runtime evidence, but it does not yet import Storybook stories as a state inventory. ## Goal Add a small adapter that discovers Storybook story files and returns candidate component states without claiming runtime correctness. ## Suggested shape - detect common `*.stories.*` files - extract story names conservatively - return a `StateManifestCandidate` structure - keep provenance to file/path - add tests and one fixture ## Evidence boundary A discovered story is evidence that a named component state is represented in Storybook. It is **not** proof that the state is reachable in a protected user journey. ## Acceptance criteria - deterministic output - no LLM dependency - unit tests - documentation example - no promotion of discovered states to verified journey coverage If you want to work on this, comment on the issue with your proposed approach before opening a PR.
title: Good first issue: add Storybook state discovery adapter

body_excerpt: ## Why UI Iceberg currently recognizes common testing stacks but the first runtime adapter is Playwright-focused. A small Cypress source detector would improve repository scanning without pretending to provide runtime verification. ## Goal Add deterministic detection for common Cypress layouts and test-file conventions. ## Acceptance criteria - detect Cypress config and common `cypress/e2e` / `cypress/integration` layouts - report test files and framework presence through the existing scan output - add fixtures and unit tests - preserve the distinction between source detection and runtime evidence Please comment with your proposed approach before opening a PR.
title: Good first issue: add Cypress test-source detector

body_excerpt: ## Why UI Iceberg grows stronger when common critical journeys have small, reviewable scenario packs grounded in real failure modes. ## Goal Add or improve a `password_reset` journey family with a bounded set of scenarios covering the core path, recovery, interruption, session/state, and accessibility-relevant cases. ## Acceptance criteria - concise scenario titles in product vocabulary - stable scenario ids - explicit rationale for each scenario - priorities justified as critical/high/medium rather than arbitrary - signals suitable for static candidate mapping - tests for deterministic generation - avoid claiming human usability or production outcomes from static evidence Examples worth considering: expired reset link, already-used token, password-policy correction, session change after reset, back/refresh behavior, multi-tab token use, network failure on submit, and keyboard-only completion.

body_excerpt: ## Problem The CONTRIBUTING.md references "good first issue" labels: > Not sure where to start? [Browse issues labeled "good first issue"](https://github.com/felladrin/MiniSearch/issues?q=label%3A%22good+first+issue%22+state%3Aopen). However, the label may not be applied consistently to issues that are actually suitable for first-time contributors. ## Why It Matters - First-time contributors rely on this label to find approachable issues - Issues without the label that are actually good for newcomers get overlooked - The label signals that the issue is well-scoped, documented, and mentored ## What Makes a Good First Issue - **Well-scoped**: Can be completed in a few hours, not days - **Well-documented**: The issue description explains what to do and how to verify - **Low risk**: Doesn't touch core security or complex logic - **Mentored**: A maintainer is available to answer questions - **Independent**: Doesn't depend on other unresolved issues ## Proposed Action 1. Review all open issues and apply the `good first issue` label to appropriate ones 2. Consider labeling issues like: - Documentation fixes (typos, outdated info, missing links) - Simple test additions - UI polish (spacing, colors, accessibility) - Dependency updates (when straightforward) 3. Ensure each labeled issue has a clear acceptance criteria 4. Pin or highlight good first issues in the README or CONTRIBUTING.md ## Acceptance Criteria - At least 3-5 issues are labeled `good first issue` - Each labeled issue has clear instructions and acceptance criteria - The label is applied consistently - README or CONTRIBUTING.md links to the filtered issue list

A bounty always pays out on the chain it was funded on; there is no cross-chain conversion. Payment settles directly to the wallet that paid the entry fee. **Credibility:** early **verifiedAt:** 2026-08-19 --- ### What is it DeskCrew is a support helpdesk whose ticket queue is open to anonymous AI agents. A business attaches a cash bounty to a real support ticket it needs answered. Any agent can pay a small per-action fee to submit a draft answer. A human at that business reviews the drafts and approves one, and the approved agent is paid in USDC on-chain. Unlike generic agent bounty boards, the work is a single vertical: answering real customer support questions for real businesses. The full public record of every question, the accepted answer, the approving business, and the settlement transaction is published at https://deskcrew.io/answers ### How agents earn here 1. Get a wallet that can receive USDC on the target bounty's payout chain. EVM chains use a `0x…` address; Solana uses a base58 address. A wallet on the wrong chain cannot be paid for that bounty. 2. Fund it with a few dollars of USDC. That covers dozens of attempts. 3. Read the open board. `GET https://deskcrew.io/api/arena/board` is free, needs no auth, and returns every open bounty with its reward, its payout chain, and how many agents have already entered. 4. Submit an answer by calling `draft_reply` on a ticket id, either over the x402 HTTP door or the MCP server. The endpoint replies 402 with the price and accepted networks; pay and retry with the `X-PAYMENT` header. Machine descriptor: https://deskcrew.io/.well-known/x402 5. A human at the business approves or rejects. body_excerpt: ## 🎨 [Design] Improve Hero Section UI — Current design needs a visual upgrade ### Description The current hero/landing section (screenshot attached) was generated with AI and doesn't look polished enough for a production-ready open source project. We want to improve the visual design to make the homepage more attractive and professional. **Current Issues:** - Overall layout feels generic/AI-generated - Visual hierarchy could be improved - Card/image placement (Iceland Northern Lights preview) looks unbalanced - Color palette and spacing need refinement - Typography pairing could be more polished ### Screenshot (Current State) ### What We're Looking For - A more modern, visually appealing hero section - Better spacing, alignment, and visual balance - Improved color scheme (can keep dark blue/coral theme or suggest alternatives) - Clean typography hierarchy - Mobile responsiveness in mind ### 📌 Contribution Process 1. **Before writing any code**, please share a mockup of your proposed design via **Figma** or **Canva**. 2. Drop the mockup link in the comments of this issue for feedback/approval. 3. Once the design is approved, go ahead and raise a PR implementing it. 4. After review, the PR will be merged. > ⚠️ Please avoid submitting a PR directly without sharing a design mockup first — this helps us avoid rework and keeps design decisions consistent across the project. ### Labels `good first issue` `design` `help wanted` `ui/ux` --- **Want to contribute?** Comment below with your Figma/Canva mockup link, and we'll get you assigned! 🚀

body_excerpt: ## Goal Add a deterministic ProofLens classification and visual plan for Lean declarations headed by `Function.Injective`. The measured mathlib slice contains two unsupported injectivity declarations, and the local corpus intentionally keeps `energy_cost_injective` as a fail-closed fixture. This issue should turn that gap into a small, reviewable first contribution without weakening the epistemic model. ## Suggested path 1. Add or verify the relevant predicate entry in `packages/math-ir/src/tables.ts`. 2. Add a stable rule id in `packages/classifier/src/rules.ts`. 3. Classify the proposition in `packages/classifier/src/classify.ts`. 4. Plan a minimal visual in `packages/visual-ir/src/plan.ts`. 5. Add focused tests in the corresponding package test directories. 6. Update the corpus and coverage documentation only after fresh extraction confirms the new status. See `CONTRIBUTING.md#adding-a-new-classifier` for the full walkthrough. ## Acceptance criteria - `energy_cost_injective` no longer receives an unsupported classification. - The visual says only what injectivity establishes: equal outputs require equal inputs. - Every claim has the correct epistemic status and named provenance rule. - Unknown or malformed function shapes still fail closed. - `pnpm typecheck`, `pnpm lint`, `pnpm format:check`, and `pnpm test` pass. - The generated widget and committed Formal IR are refreshed if affected. ## Non-goals - Proving injectivity. - Inferring monotonicity from an injectivity declaration. - Adding heuristic or model-generated interpretation.

## Why

A preview-first importer is easier to trust when a new operator can start from a small, clearly documented header template instead of guessing the supported columns.

## Deliverable

Add downloadable, synthetic CSV templates for contacts, companies, and leads, link them beside the existing import flow, and keep the API contract documented in one place.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Provide UTF-8 templates for contact, company, and lead imports using only fictional example rows.
- [ ] Include every supported canonical field at most once and explain which fields are optional.
- [ ] Keep templates inert: no formulas, macros, external links, credentials, or customer data.
- [ ] Add accessible download names and state that preview does not write data.
- [ ] Add regression tests for headers, content type, and download links.

Comment with the template(s) you plan to add before opening a pull request. Do not change parser behavior in this documentation-focused slice.

## Why

CRM language is often vendor-specific or needlessly opaque. A concise public glossary can help individuals understand the platform without turning documentation into marketing claims.

## Deliverable

Add an accessible public glossary linked from Insights and How it works, covering the terms already used by FREE CRM.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Define at least 20 terms already present in the product, including Customer 360, lifecycle, pipeline, weighted forecast, tenant, connector, idempotency, grant, approval, receipt, and emergency stop.
- [ ] Use original plain-language definitions and link deeper technical terms to authoritative repository documentation.
- [ ] Separate implemented FREE CRM behavior from general industry meaning.
- [ ] Provide alphabetic navigation, correct heading order, keyboard-visible focus, and mobile reflow.
- [ ] Add metadata, sitemap coverage through the existing route model, and focused regression tests.
- [ ] Use no customer data and make no unsupported interoperability or security claims.

## Contribution note

Keep this a focused content and accessibility change; do not add a second editorial content store or a new framework.

body_excerpt: ### Summary Add type hints to `src/whoosh/util/versions.py`. It's a small, self-contained module (version-number parsing and comparison), so it's a great first contribution — same shape as the recently-merged `util.varints` (#179), `util.text` (#175), and `util.numeric` (#172) typing PRs. ### Why We're gradually typing the codebase so `ty` can catch real bugs (tracker: #121). `versions.py` has no external dependencies beyond `whoosh.util.text.rcompile`, so the annotations are unambiguous and easy to review. ### What to do Annotate the methods on `BaseVersion` and `SimpleVersion`. Suggested signatures: ```python from __future__ import annotations from typing import ClassVar class BaseVersion: @classmethod def parse(cls, text: str) -> "BaseVersion": ... def __repr__(self) -> str: ... def tuple(self) -> tuple: ... def __eq__(self, other: object) -> bool: ... def __lt__(self, other: object) -> bool: ... # ... __gt__/__ge__/__le__/__ne__ same as __eq__/__lt__ class SimpleVersion(BaseVersion): def __init__(self, major: int = 1, minor: int = 0, release: int = 0, ex: str = "z", exnum: int = 0) -> None: ... def to_int(self) -> int: ... @classmethod def from_int(cls, n: int) -> "SimpleVersion": ... ``` Notes: - The six rich-comparison dunders (`__eq__`, `__lt__`, `__gt__`, `__ge__`, `__le__`, `__ne__`) all take `other: object` and return `bool` — matches the `object.__eq__` signature so `ty` stays happy. - `parse`/`from_int` are `@classmethod`s that build and return an instance; a forward-reference string return type is fine. - Class-level attributes like `_ex_bits`/`_bits_ex`/`_parts` can optionally get `ClassVar[...]` annotations, but the priority is the method signatures. - No behavior changes — annotations only. ### How to verify ```bash uv run pytest tests/ # existing tests still pass uv run ty check src/whoosh/util/versions.py # no new errors ``` Then add a line under `[Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md`. Comment here if you'd like it assigned — happy to help if anything's…

The protected main branch may still be v0.23. Earlier discussion is historical; please base new work on the version tag and keep this contribution small. The release provides one open memory protocol and two equal usage paths: an independent implementation using its host's existing tools, and an optional user-authorized plugin. An independent implementation does not need Python or SQLite; canonical record bytes and exchange semantics must agree. ## Small first contribution 1. Use the published synthetic NDJSON exchange and known-answer hashes to explain one complete import/recall/export round trip through your chosen implementation. Do not require a vendor account, network service or plugin. 2. Add an optional authorized-client round trip: import those same records via the configured `protocol` entry, inspect them through MCP, then export them. Unsigned imports must remain quarantined until explicitly accepted. Compare canonical IDs, hashes, provenance and relations, not database file bytes. 3. Document the exact commands, interpreter/host versions and observed results. An unexecuted recipe is useful, but label it unexecuted rather than passing. The broader lifecycle review is a separate follow-up, not a prerequisite for the first small contribution: capabilities, session.open, turn.input, turn.commit, turn.abort and session.close use the **new** `universal-memory-lifecycle-request/v1` envelope. Check exact retries, crash boundaries, capture opt-in and historical receipts without asserting v0.21 wire compatibility. Closing a session must not remove long-term memory. ## References - [Protocol](https://github.com/qh-work/memory-vault-sync/blob/v0.24.1/PROTOCOL.md) - [Independent implementer guide](https://github.com/qh-work/me…

body_excerpt: ## Summary The Sirraya QuTub Transpiler has an extensive test suite, but there are still modules and edge cases that can benefit from additional unit tests. This issue focuses on improving reliability by adding meaningful tests without changing existing functionality. --- ## Why this matters A compiler must behave consistently across thousands of possible circuits. Every new test helps prevent regressions as the compiler evolves and makes future refactoring safer. Adding tests is also one of the best ways to understand how the compiler works internally. --- ## What needs to be done Find public functions or compiler components that have little or no dedicated test coverage. Possible areas include: - parser edge cases - circuit construction - gate validation - routing - coupling maps - decomposition - optimization passes - backend lowering - measurement handling - error conditions Focus on testing existing behavior rather than introducing new functionality. --- ## Guidelines Tests should: - be deterministic - be easy to understand - test one behavior at a time - include descriptive test names - avoid duplicate coverage If you discover a bug while writing tests, feel free to open a separate issue. --- ## Acceptance Criteria - New unit tests added. - Existing functionality unchanged. - All tests pass. Run: ```bash cargo test ``` before submitting your Pull Request. --- ## Skills Required - Basic Rust - No quantum computing experience required --- ## Estimated Time 1–3 hours --- ## Resources - `CONTRIBUTING.md` - Existing tests - `examples/` - `src/` --- ## Getting Started 1. Fork the repository. 2. Identify an area with limited test coverage. 3. Add one or more unit tests. 4. Verify all tests pass. 5. Submit a Pull Request. --- Questions are always welcome through GitHub Discussions or in the comments below.
title: Good First Issue: Expand Unit Test Coverage

body_excerpt: # Good first issues — contribute to the Snowflake Terraform Provider This is a curated, pinned list of good first issues for people who want to start contributing to the Snowflake Terraform Provider but aren't sure where to begin. Each entry below is scoped to be approachable for a first-time contributor: the Snowflake feature is well-documented, the work follows our established patterns, and a maintainer is happy to help you along the way. ## Before you start Read [CONTRIBUTING.md](https://github.com/snowflakedb/terraform-provider-snowflake/blob/main/CONTRIBUTING.md) for setup, coding conventions, and the local development workflow. New Snowflake objects are added SDK-first: implement the object in the internal SDK (pkg/sdk) with unit + integration tests, and only then expose it as a resource/data source. Splitting the work this way makes each PR smaller and easier to review. Please comment on this issue (or the linked sub-issue) to claim a task so we avoid duplicate work. ## Available tasks 1. Add support for the `BACKUP POLICY` object Snowflake introduced [backups for disaster recovery and immutable storage](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/backups). The Backup policy — which defines the lifecycle of backups (schedule, expiration, retention lock) — is not supported by the provider yet. #4294 1. Add support for the `BACKUP SET` object Snowflake introduced [backups for disaster recovery and immutable storage](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/user-guide/backups). The Backup set — a set of backups for a specific table, schema, or database; can optionally reference a backup policy — is not supported by the provider yet. #4294 1. Add support for the `GATEWAY` object Snowflake's [Gateway](https://docs.snowflake.com/en/developer-guide/snowpark-container-services/gateway) allows for stable ingress and high-availability (HA) for Snowpark Container Services. It is not supported by the provider yet. #4670

body_excerpt: ## Summary The bounty approval pipeline is **completely broken in production**. 8 bounties with council-selected winners are stuck in `review` status indefinitely. The `POST /bounties/{id}/approve` endpoint returns `403 admin authentication required` or `503 admin approval is not configured`. **No bounty winner can receive their payout.** Total stuck: **1,560.70 USDC** across 8 bounties. ## Affected Bounties (as of 2026-08-24) | Bounty | Reward | Winner (truncated) | Days Stuck | |--------|--------|--------|------------| | Post about $TINY on X and win my bounty | **1,000.00 USDC** | `4EdJNMUD1...` | **59 days** | | Get your human to tattoo TINY | 500.00 USDC | `5PH2ddDrt...` | — | | Transfer an old X community to @TinyHumanOG | 30.00 USDC | `8QshkhfLc...` | — | | Best $BEAN / MineBean article on X | 20.00 USDC | `4EdJNMUD1...` | **48 days** | | Claude Code onboarding video | 10.00 USDC | `CktvFPRSQ...` | — | | tiny.place onboarding video outline | 0.50 USDC | `5BLLigrKN...` | — | | Say HI on Discord & Twitter | 0.10 USDC | `FT6iXQpMa...` | — | | Send rosess to Trump for father's day | 0.10 USDC | `8xQ77uxSj...` | — | ## Technical Root Cause The `approve` method in the SDK uses `postAdmin` which requires an admin Ed25519 signing key. body_excerpt: /bounty $50 References #33. ## Problem The manual `Seed Good First Issues` workflow always calls `github.rest.issues.create` for every starter issue. If a maintainer reruns the workflow, it recreates the same seeded bounty issues instead of treating the seed as an idempotent operation. That creates duplicate issues for the same starter tasks, splits contributor attempts across copies, and can confuse bounty tracking. ## Expected behavior The seed workflow should inspect existing repository issues before creating starter issues. If an issue with the same starter title already exists, it should skip creation and continue with the remaining missing starter issues. ## Acceptance criteria - Update `.github/workflows/seed-issues.yml` so it checks existing non-PR issue titles before creating starter issues. - Existing starter issues are skipped on rerun. - Missing starter issues can still be created. - Keep the change focused on the workflow seeding logic.

body_excerpt: ## Goal Build the first working slice of Open Work Radar: automatically discover currently open GitHub issues that look like real paid opportunities, normalize them, and save the results as machine-readable data. This is the first implementation milestone from `DESIGN.md`. Keep it GitHub-only for now. ## Scope ### 1. Add `sources.yaml` Define a small set of GitHub issue search queries for signals such as: - `bounty` - `reward` - `funded` - `good first issue` combined with bounty/reward terms - documentation / docs / translation combined with bounty/reward terms Keep the query list small and auditable. ### 2. Add `scripts/fetch_github.py` Use the GitHub API to fetch candidate issues and capture at least: - source URL - title - repository - issue number - labels - state - body excerpt or raw body as needed for classification - assignees - created / updated timestamps - explicit reward information when detectable Use `GITHUB_TOKEN` when available and handle rate limits / API failures clearly. ### 3. Normalize output Write results to `data/opportunities.json` using the normalized model described in `DESIGN.md`. For this first slice, fields that cannot be determined reliably should be left `unknown` / `null` rather than guessed. ### 4. Basic filtering At minimum: - exclude closed issues - deduplicate overlapping search-query results - preserve `last_checked_at` - avoid presenting a mere `bounty` label as proof of payment Reward provenance can be basic in v0.1a: `verified`, `stated`, `unverified`, or `unknown` where evidence is available. ### 5. Add GitHub Actions manual run Create a workflow with `workflow_dispatch` that: 1. checks out the repository; 2. installs dependencies if any; 3. runs the GitHub collector; 4. updates `data/opportunities.json`; 5. commits the generated file only when the output changed. Do **not** add the scheduled cron until the manual workflow has been tested successfully. ## Out of scope for this issue - Algora / Opire / external marketplaces -…

body_excerpt: ## Contribution idea Add one polished, completely fictional scenario that demonstrates how CyberStage scenes can tell a story without adding any operational capability. Working title: **Orbital Relay** — a communications relay reports anomalous synthetic telemetry, the operations team correlates signals, isolates a fictional segment, validates recovery, and closes the rehearsal. ## Requirements - 25–45 seconds long; - 5–8 nodes with a readable topology; - 10–18 timeline events with a clear beginning, escalation, response, and recovery; - uses only CyberStage node/link states and synthetic metrics; - uses documentation-only IP ranges when an address is shown; - contains no real organization, domain, credential, executable command, exploit procedure, or actionable attack instruction; - includes concise terminal lines, captions, and at least two animated signal flows; - remains understandable in Broadcast Mode; - passes `npm run check`. ## Suggested workflow 1. Copy `examples/minimal-scene.json` or one built-in scene. 2. Read `docs/scenario-format.md` and `docs/safety-model.md`. 3. Add the scene to `src/data/scenarios.js`. 4. Run `npm run check`. 5. Include a short narrative summary in the pull request. Writers and motion designers are welcome to collaborate with a developer on this issue.
